why_how.text: Keeping right leaves the left side for passing and oncoming traffic, so leaving it needs a listed reason.
Slow vehicles stay right so faster traffic can pass safely.
Only emergency and police vehicles with lights and sirens may drive against traffic.

scenario.text: On a two-lane road, Priya finds a stalled car blocking her lane.

reasoning.text: An obstacle can force you over the center line, but you must yield to oncoming traffic first.

result.text: Priya waits for oncoming cars to pass, then goes around the stalled car and returns to the right lane.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you may only leave the right lane to pass.

correction.text: Multi-lane roads, one-way streets, directing signs, stopped emergency vehicles and construction also allow it.

prompt.text: You are driving a slow farm vehicle and want to turn left soon. Which lane do you use until then?

answer.text: The right lane, leaving it only to pass or to turn left.

rationale.text: Slow vehicles must stay in the right lane except to pass or turn left.

lines.text: The right lane is home base.

narration.text: This lesson is about choosing your lane. In Michigan, the basic rule is to drive in the right-hand lane. That keeps the left side open for passing and for traffic coming the other way. But there are many good reasons to leave the right lane, and the handbook lists them. We will go through the general rule, the road layouts and signs that allow you to move left, the emergency and construction cases, the rule for slow vehicles, and who may drive against traffic. Practice questions often ask whether a reason is on the list, so knowing the list is the goal.

lines.text: Leave it to pass or avoid obstacles.

narration.text: Drive in the right-hand lane unless you are passing, or stopped vehicles, a crash or another obstacle forces you over the center line. When that happens, you must yield to oncoming traffic first. So an obstacle gives you permission to cross, but it does not give you the right of way. Oncoming drivers are still in their own lane, and you are the one entering it. Wait for a safe gap, move around the obstacle, and come back to the right as soon as you can. The rule is short, but it covers most everyday driving on two-lane roads.

lines.text: One-way streets with two or more lanes.
Signs or signals directing you left.

narration.text: Leaving the right lane is also allowed in three road situations. The first is a road with three or more marked lanes. The second is a one-way street with two or more lanes. The third is when signs or signals on a two-way multi-lane highway direct you left. In each case, the road itself is built or marked so that using other lanes is expected. A separate case covers crossing the center line to turn. You may cross the center line to turn left into or out of an alley, private road or driveway. That is how you reach places on the other side of the road.

lines.text: Go around a stopped emergency vehicle.

narration.text: You may leave the right lane to go around a stopped emergency vehicle once it is safe. You may also leave it when road construction is near or blocking the right lane or shoulder. These cases protect people working on or beside the road. Moving over gives responders and crews space. The words once it is safe matter. Going around a stopped emergency vehicle does not mean swerving out at speed. It means checking traffic, slowing as needed, and moving over when the lane beside you is clear. Treat a work zone or a crash scene as a reason to move away, and to move carefully.

lines.text: Except to pass or turn left.
Only lights and sirens go against traffic.

narration.text: Slow vehicles must stay in the right lane except to pass or turn left. That lets faster traffic pass on the left without weaving around them. If you are driving something slow, such as a heavily loaded vehicle, keep right until you need to turn left. One more lane rule is about direction. Only emergency and police vehicles running lights and sirens may drive against the flow of traffic. No other driver may do this, no matter how empty the road looks or how short the distance is. Driving against traffic is reserved for emergencies, and even then only with lights and sirens on.

title.text: Passing is not the only reason

lines.text: Trap: you leave the right lane only to pass.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many people think the only reason to leave the right lane is to pass. That is wrong. Leaving the right lane is also allowed on roads with three or more marked lanes, on one-way streets with two or more lanes, and when signs or signals direct you left. And you may leave it to go around a stopped emergency vehicle once it is safe, or for construction near or blocking the right lane. So an option claiming that passing is the only reason misses most of the list. When a question names a road layout, a sign, a responder or a work zone, it is pointing to an allowed reason.

lines.text: A slow vehicle on a two-lane road.
A left turn is coming up.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are driving a slow farm vehicle on a road, and you will turn left a little way ahead. Which lane do you use until then? Recall the rule for slow vehicles. Slow vehicles must stay in the right lane except to pass or to turn left. So you stay in the right lane now, and move left only when it is time to make the turn. Moving left early would hold up faster traffic and invite unsafe passing. Staying right until the turn keeps the road flowing and keeps you predictable to the drivers behind you.

To finish, drive in the right-hand lane unless you are passing or an obstacle forces you over the center line, and then yield to oncoming traffic first. You may also leave the right lane on roads with three or more marked lanes, on one-way streets with two or more lanes, when signs or signals direct you left, to go around a stopped emergency vehicle once it is safe, or for construction. You may cross the center line to turn into or out of an alley, private road or driveway. Slow vehicles keep right, and only emergency and police vehicles with lights and sirens drive against traffic.

why_how.text: Freeways move fast, so the left lane is held for listed reasons and weaving is banned.
Medians separate traffic, so only a paved cut-through without a prohibiting sign may be used to turn.
Controlled-access roads are entered and left only where entrances and exits are posted.
An empty freeway left lane, with no one right behind or ahead, is a listed reason to be there; weaving never is.

scenario.text: On an interstate, Ken sees a crash on the right shoulder and a work crew ahead.

reasoning.text: You may use the freeway left lane to move over for emergency or construction vehicles.

result.text: Ken moves to the left lane to give room, then returns right once past.

claim.text: Myth: any median may be crossed when traffic is light.

correction.text: Driving across median strips or through barriers is illegal; only a paved cut-through with no prohibiting sign may be used for a left turn.

prompt.text: On a quiet interstate, a driver stays in the left lane with no cars right behind or ahead. Is that a listed reason?

answer.text: Yes, an empty left lane is a listed reason, though weaving never is.

rationale.text: On freeways you may use the left lane when no traffic is right behind or ahead of you, but weaving through traffic is illegal.

narration.text: This lesson covers freeways and medians. On interstates and full-access controlled freeways, the keep-right rule is stricter than on ordinary roads, and the left lane is used only for listed reasons. We will go through those reasons, the ban on weaving, the rule for median strips and paved cut-throughs, and where you may enter and leave controlled-access roads. Freeway speeds leave less room for error, which is why these rules are firm. Practice questions often present a reason for being in the left lane and ask whether it is allowed, so the list itself is what you want to remember.

lines.text: Left lane for congestion or weather.
Or a hazard in the right lane.

narration.text: On an interstate or full-access controlled freeway, you must keep right. You may use the left lane only when congestion or weather requires it, or when an obstacle or hazard sits in the right lane. So the freeway rule starts from the right lane and lists the exceptions. Heavy traffic can spread drivers across every lane. Bad weather can make one lane safer than another. A hazard in the right lane can force you over. Outside those cases, the right lane is where you belong, and the left lane stays open for the traffic that needs it, such as drivers passing.

lines.text: Or when no one is near you.

narration.text: On those same freeways, you may also use the left lane to move over for emergency or construction vehicles. This gives responders and crews room on the shoulder or in the right lane. You may also use the left lane when no traffic is right behind or ahead of you in that lane. That last reason is easy to forget. If the left lane is empty around you, being there is a listed reason. But once traffic comes up behind you, the reason is gone, and you should move back to the right. Think of the left lane as borrowed space that you return when others need it.

lines.text: No crossing median strips or barriers.
Paved cut-through, if no sign forbids.

narration.text: Driving across median strips or through barriers is illegal. But you may turn left through a paved median cut-through when no sign forbids it. So the difference is the paved cut-through and the absence of a prohibiting sign. A grass median is not a road, and a barrier is there to stop vehicles, not to be driven around. Controlled-access roads have a matching rule. Enter and leave them only at designated, posted entrances and exits. You may not create your own exit across a shoulder or through a gap. The road tells you where you may get on and off.

lines.text: Trap: an empty lane allows weaving.
Empty left lane: a listed reason.

narration.text: Here is the trap. On a freeway, an empty left lane with no one right behind or ahead of you is a listed reason you may drive there, while weaving through traffic is never allowed. Weaving between lanes to speed through traffic is illegal. Options may suggest that weaving is fine when traffic is light, or that signaling each lane change makes it legal. Both are wrong. Using an empty left lane means staying in one lane where no one is near you. Weaving means darting between lanes to get ahead. The first is allowed by the list. The second is banned outright.

lines.text: No cars right behind or ahead.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: on a quiet interstate, a driver stays in the left lane, and there are no cars right behind or ahead of her in that lane. Is that a listed reason to be there? Recall the freeway list. You may use the left lane for congestion or weather, for a right-lane hazard, to move over for emergency or construction vehicles, or when no traffic is right behind or ahead of you. Her lane is empty around her, so the answer is yes. But if she began weaving between lanes to get ahead, that would be illegal, whatever the traffic.

To finish, on interstates and full-access controlled freeways you must keep right, using the left lane only for congestion, weather or a right-lane hazard, to move over for emergency or construction vehicles, or when no traffic is right behind or ahead of you. Weaving between lanes to speed through traffic is illegal. Driving across median strips or through barriers is illegal, but a paved median cut-through with no prohibiting sign may be used for a left turn. And you enter and leave controlled-access roads only at designated, posted entrances and exits. The hook is cut-through yes, median no.

why_how.text: Turns cross other people's paths, so each one starts with the right lane, a signal and yielding.
Matching lanes in double turns keeps two drivers from colliding side by side.
Wheels kept straight while waiting mean a rear-end crash will not push you into oncoming traffic.

scenario.text: Ana waits in the intersection to turn left while oncoming traffic passes.

reasoning.text: Keep your front wheels straight until you begin the turn, and check for hidden motorcycles, scooters and bicycles.

result.text: Ana keeps her wheels straight, spots a motorcycle behind a van, waits, then turns.

claim.text: Common mistake: turning your wheels left early so you are ready to go.

correction.text: While waiting to turn left, hold the front wheels straight and turn them only as the turn begins.

prompt.text: You are in the outer of two left-turn lanes. Where should your turn end?

answer.text: In the lane on the new road that corresponds to your turn lane.

rationale.text: Ending in the matching lane keeps you from cutting off the driver turning beside you.

narration.text: This lesson is about making right and left turns. Turns are where your path crosses the paths of pedestrians, bicyclists and other drivers, so each turn follows a set of steps. We will cover the right turn, including following the curb and giving large vehicles room, then the left turn, including wheel position and scanning for road users who are easy to miss. We will also look at intersections with two turn lanes side by side. Practice questions in this area usually test one step of the turn, so learning the steps in order will help you see which one a question is asking about.

lines.text: Check that your left is clear.

narration.text: For a right turn, use the correct lane and your signal, and obey signs and signals. Yield to pedestrians, emergency vehicles and other traffic. Then check that your left side is clear. That last check matters because traffic approaching from the left is the traffic you will pull in front of. During the turn, follow the curve of the curb and stay out of other lanes. Do not swing wide into the next lane, and do not cut across the far lane to finish quickly. A tight, predictable right turn keeps you in your own space and lets drivers around you know where you are going.

lines.text: Trucks and buses need extra room.
Give them space at right turns.

narration.text: Trucks and buses need extra room to turn right. A long vehicle cannot follow the curb the way a car does, so it may start the turn from farther out, or use part of another lane. If you are beside or behind a truck or bus at a right turn, give it space. Do not squeeze into the gap between a turning truck and the curb, because that gap can close as the truck finishes its turn. Hang back until the turn is complete. This is one of the simplest rules in the lesson, and it prevents some of the most serious side crashes at intersections.

For a left turn, use the correct lane and signal, obey signs and signals, and yield to pedestrians, bicyclists, emergency vehicles and other traffic. Keep your front wheels pointed straight until you actually begin the turn. The reason is safety. If your wheels are already turned and someone hits you from behind, you can be pushed into oncoming traffic. With your wheels straight, you are pushed forward instead. Before you go, check all approaching traffic, and look for vehicles hidden behind or beside others, especially motorcycles, scooters and bicycles, which are easy to miss.

lines.text: Two right lanes: finish in your match.
Two left lanes: end in your match.

narration.text: Some intersections have two turn lanes side by side. With multiple right-turn lanes, finish the turn in the lane that matches the one you turned from, since drifting can cut off another driver and cause a crash. With multiple left-turn lanes, end the turn in the lane that corresponds to your turn lane. So the inner lane leads to the inner lane, and the outer lane leads to the outer lane. The driver beside you is turning at the same time, along a path right next to yours. Staying in your matching lane keeps both of you in your own space through the whole turn.

lines.text: Trap: turn your wheels while waiting.
Turn them as the turn begins.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers turn their wheels left while they wait, so they feel ready to go. That is wrong. While waiting to turn left, hold the front wheels straight ahead and turn them only as the turn begins. Options may say that turning your wheels early saves time, or that wheel position does not matter. Both are wrong. The risk is being hit from behind while waiting. With turned wheels, the push sends you into oncoming traffic. With straight wheels, it sends you forward. This is a small habit that protects you during the moment you are most exposed.

lines.text: You are in the outer one.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are in the outer of two left-turn lanes at a busy intersection. Where should your turn end? Recall the double turn rule. With multiple left-turn lanes, end the turn in the lane that corresponds to your turn lane. So the outer turn lane leads to the outer lane on the new road. Ending in the matching lane prevents you from cutting off the driver turning beside you in the inner lane. If you drifted into the inner lane, you would cross directly into that driver's path, which is how side crashes in double turns happen.

lines.text: Left: wheels straight, scan for bikes.

narration.text: To finish, every turn starts with the correct lane, a signal, obeying signs and signals, and yielding. On a right turn, check that your left side is clear, follow the curve of the curb, stay out of other lanes, and give trucks and buses extra room. On a left turn, yield to pedestrians, bicyclists, emergency vehicles and other traffic, keep your wheels straight until the turn begins, and scan for motorcycles, scooters and bicycles hidden behind other vehicles. In double turn lanes, finish in the lane that matches the one you turned from. The hook is stay in your lane.

why_how.text: Signals tell others what you are about to do, so every turn gets one.
A head check covers the blind spot on the side you are moving toward.

scenario.text: Omar needs to move one lane to the right before his exit.

reasoning.text: To move right, check behind and to your right, signal right, and move over carefully.

result.text: Omar checks his right side, signals right, and moves over smoothly.

claim.text: Common mistake: checking the same side no matter which way you move.

correction.text: A lane change to the left starts with a head check to your left, and a change to the right checks to your right.

prompt.text: You want to move one lane left on a busy road. What is your first step?

answer.text: Check behind and to your left with a head check.

rationale.text: To move left, head-check behind and to your left, then signal left and move over carefully.

narration.text: This lesson covers signaling and changing lanes. Signals are how you tell other road users what you are about to do, and lane changes are where many side crashes start. We will look at the rule to always signal turns, who still uses hand signals, and the steps for moving one lane to the left or to the right. The steps are the same in both directions, except for which side you check. Practice questions often swap the sides, so pay attention to that one difference. If you learn the order of check, signal and move, the rest follows naturally.

Always signal turns. A signal gives drivers, bicyclists and pedestrians time to react to what you are about to do. Hand signals for left, right and stop still exist, but today they are used mostly by motorcyclists, scooter and moped riders, and bicyclists. So if you see a rider extend an arm, read it as a signal, just as you would read a turn signal on a car. For drivers of cars, the turn signal is the normal way to signal. Use it every time, even when you think no one is around. The person you did not see is the one who most needs to know.

lines.text: Left: head check left, signal left.

narration.text: To move one lane left, check behind and to your left with a head check, signal left, and move over carefully. To move one lane right, check behind and to your right, signal right, and move over carefully. Notice the shape of both moves: check, signal, then move. The head check matters because your mirrors leave a blind spot beside and just behind your car. Turning your head briefly covers that spot. Signal after checking, so the signal reflects a move you know is possible. Then move over smoothly, without speeding up or slowing sharply in the middle of the change.

lines.text: Trap: always check the same side.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A lane change to the left starts with a head check behind and to your left, while a change to the right checks behind and to your right. Options may describe checking left before moving right, or skipping the head check because the mirrors look clear. Both are wrong. The side you check is always the side you are moving toward, because that is where the car you might hit would be. Another trap is the order. Moving first and signaling after is wrong. The steps are check, signal, then move, in both directions.

lines.text: You need the lane to your left.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are on a busy road and want to move one lane to the left. What is your first step? Recall the order for a lane change. To move left, check behind and to your left with a head check, then signal left, then move over carefully. So the first step is the head check to your left. Signaling before you know the lane is clear can mislead the drivers behind you, and moving before you check risks hitting a car in your blind spot. Check the side you are moving toward, and then let the signal tell everyone what comes next.

To finish, always signal turns. Hand signals for left, right and stop are now used mostly by motorcyclists, scooter and moped riders, and bicyclists, so read a rider's arm as a signal. To move left, check behind and to your left with a head check, signal left, and move over carefully. To move right, check behind and to your right, signal right, and move over carefully. The hook is check the side you move. Keep the order of check, signal and move the same every time, and your lane changes will be predictable to everyone around you on the road.

why_how.text: Roundabout traffic flows one way, counterclockwise, so entering drivers yield to traffic coming from the left.
Entering on a gap and merging keeps traffic moving without stops or head-on conflicts.
Pedestrians cross at entries and exits, so watch for them each time you enter or leave.

scenario.text: Beth approaches a roundabout and sees a car circling toward her from the left.

reasoning.text: Slow down, look left at the yield line, and yield to traffic from the left, entering only on a suitable gap.

result.text: Beth lets the car pass, then merges into the flow when a gap opens.

claim.text: Common mistake: turning left into a roundabout to take the short way around.

correction.text: Never turn left to enter; that puts you in front of oncoming traffic. Merge with the flow instead.

prompt.text: You reach the yield line of a roundabout. Which way do you look for traffic?

rationale.text: Traffic circles counterclockwise and comes from your left, so you look left at the yield line.

narration.text: This lesson is about entering a roundabout. A roundabout is a circular intersection where traffic moves counterclockwise around a central island. Because all traffic flows in one direction, there are no head-on turns, and the main decision at the entry is when to join. We will look at what a roundabout is, how to approach it, how to pick your lane, whom to yield to, how to enter, and why you watch for pedestrians. Practice questions often test the direction of travel and whom you yield to, so those two ideas come first. Everything else in the lesson builds on them.

lines.text: Entering drivers yield to the left.

narration.text: A roundabout is a circular intersection where traffic moves counterclockwise around a central island. Entering vehicles yield to traffic coming from the left, including bicyclists and pedestrians. So when you arrive, the traffic you must watch is already in the circle, coming toward you from your left. You do not have the right of way at the entry. The people already circulating do. This is the reverse of what some drivers expect, since many intersections give priority to the traffic on your right. In a roundabout, the flow comes from the left, and that is where your attention goes.

lines.text: Use signs and markings to pick a lane.
Slow down; stay right of the island.
Look left at the yield line.

narration.text: When approaching a roundabout, use signs and pavement markings to pick the right lane for where you want to go. Slow down, stay to the right of the center island, and look left as you reach the yield line. Picking your lane early matters because changing lanes inside the roundabout is something you should avoid. Slowing down gives you time to read the gaps. And looking left at the yield line is where you find the traffic you must yield to. Take the approach in that order: lane, speed, then a look to the left. Each step sets up a calm entry.

Enter a roundabout when a suitable gap appears, and merge with the flow. Never turn left to enter, because that puts you in front of oncoming traffic. Entering means a gentle right-hand merge into the circle, then following it counterclockwise to your exit. Even if your destination is to the left, you get there by going around, not by cutting across. As you enter, and later as you exit, watch for pedestrians crossing. Their crossings sit at the entries and exits, which is exactly where your attention may be on the traffic in the circle. Look for both before you go.

lines.text: Trap: turn left to go left.

narration.text: Here is the trap. When your exit is to the left, it can seem faster to turn left into the roundabout. That is wrong. Never turn left to enter, because that puts you in front of oncoming traffic. You enter on a suitable gap and merge with the counterclockwise flow, and the circle carries you to your exit. Another trap is the direction of yielding. Entering vehicles yield to traffic coming from the left. An option saying you yield to the right, or that entering drivers have the right of way, is wrong. Yield to the left and merge with the flow.

Here is a quick check: you have slowed down, picked your lane, and reached the yield line of a roundabout. Which way do you look for traffic? Recall the direction of the flow. Traffic in a roundabout moves counterclockwise, so vehicles already in the circle come toward you from your left. That is why you look left as you reach the yield line, and why entering drivers yield to traffic from the left. So the answer is to look left. When a suitable gap appears, you merge with the flow, and you keep an eye out for pedestrians crossing at the entry as you go.

To finish, a roundabout is a circular intersection where traffic moves counterclockwise around a central island, and entering vehicles yield to traffic coming from the left, including bicyclists and pedestrians. As you approach, use signs and pavement markings to pick your lane, slow down, stay right of the center island, and look left at the yield line. Enter when a suitable gap appears and merge with the flow, and never turn left to enter. Watch for pedestrians crossing as you enter or exit. The hook is counterclockwise, yield left, and the habit is a slow, calm approach.

why_how.text: Once you are circulating you have the right of way, so you stop only to avoid a collision.
Lane changes and stops inside the circle cause crashes, so a missed exit is fixed by going around again.
Stopping inside the circle traps you and the emergency vehicle, so you exit first and then pull over.

scenario.text: While circling, Rosa hears a siren and sees an ambulance coming up behind her.

reasoning.text: Do not stop in the roundabout; leave at the nearest exit, pull right and stop to let it pass.

result.text: Rosa takes the next exit, pulls right, stops, and returns once the ambulance is gone.

claim.text: Common mistake: stopping inside the circle when you miss your exit or hear a siren.

correction.text: A missed exit means going around again, and an emergency vehicle means leaving by the nearest exit before you stop.

prompt.text: You are circulating and a driver is waiting at the next entry. Who has the right of way?

answer.text: You do, because you are already inside the roundabout.

rationale.text: Entering drivers yield to traffic from the left, and once inside you have the right of way over drivers waiting to enter.

narration.text: This lesson follows you through a roundabout and out the other side. Once you are inside, the rules change: you now have the right of way, and the goal is to keep moving smoothly to your exit. We will cover right of way inside the circle, what to do when an emergency vehicle approaches, why you choose your lane before entering, how to treat trucks, how to exit, and what to do if you miss your exit. Practice questions often test the moments when drivers are tempted to stop or change lanes inside the circle, so we will look closely at those moments and the correct response.

lines.text: Stay right of the center island.
Circulating traffic has the right of way.
Stop only for collision or danger.

narration.text: Inside a roundabout, stay to the right of the center island. Vehicles already circulating have the right of way, and you stop only when it is the only safe way to avoid a collision. So once you are in the circle, you do not stop for drivers waiting to enter. They yield to you, just as you yielded to circulating traffic when you entered. This is the turning point of the roundabout. Entering, you yield to traffic from your left. Inside, you have the right of way over drivers waiting to enter. Stopping without a reason inside the circle surprises the drivers behind you.

lines.text: Do not pass or ride beside trucks.

narration.text: Choose your lane before entering a roundabout, and avoid changing lanes inside it. A lane change in a circle is hard to judge, because traffic around you is curving too. Trucks and trailers add another reason for care. Avoid passing or driving beside trucks and trailers in a roundabout, because they may need more than one lane to get around. And do not pass other vehicles, bicycles or mopeds inside the circle. So inside the roundabout, the plan is simple: hold your lane, keep your place in line, give large vehicles extra room, and follow the flow to your exit.

lines.text: Go slowly and signal your exit.

narration.text: You leave a roundabout by turning right onto the road you want. When exiting, keep a slow speed and signal your exit. Wait to accelerate until you are past the exit's pedestrian crossing, because people may be crossing right where you leave the circle. If you miss your exit, go around again. Going around costs only a little time, and it avoids the dangerous choices of stopping or cutting across lanes. Notice that entering and exiting mirror each other. You enter by merging with the counterclockwise flow, and you exit by turning right. You never turn left at either end.

lines.text: Do not stop in the circle.

narration.text: If an emergency vehicle approaches while you are in a roundabout, do not stop. Leave at the nearest exit, then pull right and stop to let it pass. This is different from the usual rule on an open road, where you pull over right away. In a roundabout, stopping traps both you and the emergency vehicle in the circle, and the vehicle has no room to get around you. Exiting first clears the circle. Once you are out and stopped, the emergency vehicle can move through. When it is gone, you can return to the roundabout and finish your trip.

lines.text: Trap: stop for a siren or a missed exit.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Two moments tempt drivers to stop inside a roundabout. The first is a siren. In a roundabout you do not stop for an approaching emergency vehicle; you leave by the nearest exit and only then pull right and stop. The second is a missed exit. Missing your roundabout exit is fixed by circling around again, not by stopping or changing lanes inside the circle. Options may suggest stopping right away for the siren, or cutting across to reach a missed exit. Both are wrong. In both cases the answer keeps you moving with the flow until you can leave safely.

lines.text: A driver waits at the next entry.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are circulating in a roundabout, and a driver is waiting at the next entry. Who has the right of way? Recall how right of way changes. Entering drivers yield to traffic from the left. Once you are inside, you have the right of way over drivers waiting to enter. So the answer is you. The waiting driver yields until a suitable gap appears. You keep a steady speed, stay to the right of the center island, and stop only if that is the only safe way to avoid a collision or other danger. Then you continue to your exit and leave with a right turn.

To finish, inside a roundabout you stay right of the center island, circulating traffic has the right of way, and you stop only when needed to safely avoid a collision or other danger. Choose your lane before entering, avoid lane changes inside, and do not pass or ride beside trucks, other vehicles, bicycles or mopeds. Leave by turning right, slowly and with a signal, and accelerate only past the pedestrian crossing. If you miss your exit, go around again. If an emergency vehicle approaches, leave at the nearest exit, then pull right and stop. The hook is missed it, go around.

why_how.text: Trains cannot stop quickly and are closer and faster than they look, so every crossing gets a slow look both ways.
Trains overhang the rails, so stopping too close is dangerous even when you are off the tracks.
Tracks are only safe to cross at designated crossings, and walking along or stopping on them is illegal.

scenario.text: Nia sees the railroad advance warning sign, then a train approaching the crossing.

reasoning.text: With a train coming, stop no more than fifty feet and no less than fifteen feet from the tracks.

result.text: Nia stops about twenty feet back, well clear of the overhang, and waits for the train to pass.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you are safe as long as your car is not on the rails.

correction.text: Trains overhang the rails by at least three feet on each side, and cargo can stick out farther, so stay at least fifteen feet back.

prompt.text: A driver stops five feet from the rails to get a better look at an approaching train. What is wrong?

answer.text: The stop is too close; stop at least fifteen feet from the tracks.

rationale.text: You stop between fifteen and fifty feet from the tracks, because trains overhang the rails by at least three feet.

narration.text: This lesson covers railroad crossings. Trains are heavy and fast, and they cannot stop or swerve to avoid you, so the responsibility for safety at a crossing falls on drivers, walkers and cyclists. We will look at why you slow and look at every crossing, where you may cross tracks, what the advance warning sign means, how far from the tracks you stop when a train is coming, and why trains are wider than the rails they ride on. Practice questions often test the stopping range, so we will keep those two distances clear and connect them to the reason behind them.

lines.text: A train may need a mile to stop.
Closer and faster than it looks.

narration.text: Slow down and look both ways at every railroad crossing. A train can need a mile or more to stop, so by the time the engineer sees you, it is far too late to brake. A train is also closer and faster than it looks. Its size fools the eye, making it seem to move slowly. These facts mean you cannot count on the train to avoid you, and you cannot trust a quick glance to judge its speed. Treat every crossing as a place where a train could appear, even if you cross it often and rarely see one. One careful look is worth the few seconds it takes.

Walkers, cyclists and drivers should cross tracks only at designated crossings. Walking along tracks or stopping on them is illegal. Designated crossings are where warnings, signs and sight lines are set up for people to cross. Anywhere else, there is no warning and no planned view of the approaching train. Stopping on the tracks is especially dangerous for drivers. If traffic ahead is backed up, wait before the crossing until there is room for your whole vehicle on the far side. That way you are never caught sitting on the rails if a train comes while you are waiting.

lines.text: Advance warning: a crossing is ahead.
Train coming: stop within the range.
No more than fifty, no less than fifteen.

narration.text: The railroad advance warning sign means a crossing is ahead. It is your cue to slow down and get ready to look and listen. With a train coming, stop no more than fifty feet and no less than fifteen feet from the tracks. So there is a range. Stopping farther than fifty feet back can leave you too far to see well and can confuse traffic behind you. Stopping closer than fifteen feet puts you too near the passing train. The safe place to stop is between the two. When you see the advance warning sign, start planning where in that range you will stop.

lines.text: At least three feet each side.

narration.text: Trains overhang the rails by at least three feet on each side, and cargo can stick out farther. So a train is wider than the track it runs on. This is why being off the rails is not the same as being safe. A car stopped just beside the tracks can still be struck by the side of a passing train or by its load. Picture the train as a wide box moving along the rails, with its sides reaching out past them, and leave plenty of space between that box and the front of your vehicle.

lines.text: Trap: off the rails means safe.
Stay at least fifteen feet back.

narration.text: Here is the trap. At a railroad crossing with a train coming, you stop between fifteen and fifty feet from the tracks, and the lower limit matters since trains overhang the rails by at least three feet. Options may suggest stopping right at the edge of the rails, or say any distance is fine once you are off the tracks. Both are wrong. Another trap is stopping far beyond the range, such as one hundred feet back. The rule sets both a near limit and a far limit. Keep both facts in mind: stop fifteen to fifty feet back, and remember that trains and cargo extend past the rails.

lines.text: Driver stops five feet from rails.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a driver stops five feet from the rails to get a better look at an approaching train. What is wrong? Recall the stopping range and the reason behind its near limit. With a train coming, you stop no more than fifty feet and no less than fifteen feet from the tracks. Five feet is inside the near limit, and trains overhang the rails by at least three feet on each side, with cargo that can stick out farther. So the stop is too close. The driver should be at least fifteen feet back, where the train and its load can pass safely.

To finish, slow down and look both ways at every railroad crossing, because a train can need a mile or more to stop and is closer and faster than it looks. Cross tracks only at designated crossings, and never walk along or stop on them. The railroad advance warning sign means a crossing is ahead, and with a train coming you stop no more than fifty feet and no less than fifteen feet from the tracks. Trains also overhang the rails by at least three feet on each side, and cargo can stick out farther. The hook is fifty to fifteen feet.
